mode_selection.title: Choosing an Operation Mode
mode_selection.body:
This determines what the script will actually DO to your files.

Most users want MIGRATE — it copies your Desktop, Documents, Pictures etc.
to a new drive and tells Windows the new location.

Do NOT choose Rollback or RepairTransactions unless something went wrong
with a previous run. Those are recovery tools, not normal operations.
mode_selection.risk: LOW — you cannot break anything at the selection screen.
mode_selection.example: You bought a new D: drive and want to move Documents off C:\. Choose 1 (Migrate).

user_selection.title: Which Users to Process
user_selection.body:
Choosing ALL users processes every Windows account on this machine.
This is rarely needed — most people only want to move their own files.

Specific user is useful when you are an admin moving files for someone else
who is not logged in.
user_selection.risk: MEDIUM — migrating ALL users takes much longer and touches other accounts.
user_selection.example: You are IT moving files for the user 'jsmith'. Choose 2, enter: jsmith

destination_path.title: Destination Path
destination_path.body:
This is WHERE your files will be copied TO.
It should be a different drive from where your files are now.

For a local drive: D:\UserData
For a network share: \\server\share\UserData

The script creates subfolders automatically for each user.
Make sure you have enough free space — check the number shown after you enter the path.
destination_path.risk: LOW — the path is created if it doesn't exist.
destination_path.example: Your Documents are on C:\. You want to move them to D:\. Enter: D:\UserData
destination_path.recommended: A different physical drive from C:\ for best results

folder_selection.title: Which Folders to Migrate
folder_selection.body:
Shell folders are the special Windows folders: Desktop, Documents, Downloads,
Music, Pictures, Videos, Favorites, Contacts, and more.

Choosing ALL is almost always correct — it ensures nothing is missed.
Selecting specific folders is useful if, for example, your Music is already
on the right drive and you only want to move Documents.
folder_selection.risk: LOW — unselected folders are simply left where they are.
folder_selection.example: Your Pictures folder is 200GB but already on D:\. Select all EXCEPT Pictures.
folder_selection.recommended: ALL — safest and most complete option

vss.title: VSS (Volume Shadow Copy Service)
vss.body:
VSS is a Windows feature that takes a snapshot of your drive so the
script can read files that are currently open or locked.

Without VSS: files locked by Outlook, browser cache, or Windows itself
will be SKIPPED during migration. You won't notice until later.

With VSS: all files are readable, even if in use. Requires Administrator rights.
VSS is automatically available on Windows 10/11.
vss.risk: LOW — enabling VSS has no downside on modern Windows.
vss.example: Outlook is running and your AppData has locked .ost files. VSS reads them anyway.
vss.recommended: Y — always use VSS unless you are sure the machine is offline

dry_run.title: Dry Run Mode
dry_run.body:
Dry Run simulates the entire migration without actually copying or changing anything.
It is completely safe — nothing on your PC is modified.

Use it to:
- Verify the script can reach the destination
- See which files would be copied and how long it would take
- Check for potential problems before committing

A full report is generated showing exactly what WOULD have happened.
dry_run.risk: ZERO — nothing changes in Dry Run mode.
dry_run.example: You are not sure if D:\ has enough space. Run in DryRun first to check.
dry_run.recommended: Y for first run on a new machine, N when you are ready to proceed

keep_source.title: Keep Source Files After Migration
keep_source.body:
After copying files to the new location, should the script leave
the original copies at the old location?

N (default): Files are copied to the new location. The originals stay.
  Windows is updated to point at the new location. Old files sit unused.
  You can delete them manually later once you confirm everything worked.

Y: Same as N, but the script also keeps registry pointing at old location.
  Use only if you need BOTH locations to work simultaneously.
keep_source.risk: LOW — this does not delete anything regardless of choice.
keep_source.example: You want to verify the new location works before deleting old files. Choose N.
keep_source.recommended: N — originals stay until you manually delete them after verification

robocopy_threads.title: Robocopy Threads
robocopy_threads.body:
Robocopy can copy multiple files simultaneously using threads.
0 = auto-detected (the script picks the best number for your hardware)

More threads = faster on fast drives (SSD, NVMe)
Fewer threads = better on slow drives (HDD, network share)

The script auto-detects your drive type and sets this optimally.
Only change this if you know what you are doing.
robocopy_threads.risk: LOW — wrong value just makes it slower, not broken.
robocopy_threads.example: You have an SSD destination and want maximum speed. Try 16.

checksum_algorithm.title: Checksum Verification Algorithm
checksum_algorithm.body:
After copying files, the script verifies each file arrived correctly
by computing a fingerprint (checksum) and comparing source vs destination.

SHA256: Most secure. Detects any bit-level corruption. Slightly slower.
SHA1:   Adequate for most migrations. Faster than SHA256.
MD5:    Fastest but very rare chance of missing corruption.

For a one-time migration of important files, SHA256 is worth the extra time.
checksum_algorithm.risk: LOW — all three catch the vast majority of copy errors.
checksum_algorithm.example: Migrating 10 years of family photos. Use SHA256 for maximum confidence.
checksum_algorithm.recommended: 1 (SHA256) — best protection, minimal speed difference on modern PCs

kfm_block.title: OneDrive KFM Block Check
kfm_block.body:
KFM stands for Known Folder Move — an OneDrive feature that keeps your
Desktop, Documents, and Pictures inside your OneDrive cloud folder.

If KFM is active and you migrate these folders to a new location,
OneDrive may silently UNDO the migration by re-redirecting the folders
back to OneDrive within seconds of the script finishing.

The KFM check detects this and shows you options to deal with it
before the migration starts. Skipping the check is only safe if you
are certain OneDrive KFM is not enabled on this machine.
kfm_block.risk: HIGH if skipped — silent OneDrive conflict can make migration appear to succeed but actually fail.
kfm_block.example: Your company uses Microsoft 365. KFM is likely active. Do NOT skip this check.
kfm_block.recommended: N (do not skip) — let the script detect and handle KFM for you

skip_registry_update.title: Skip Registry Shell Folder Update
skip_registry_update.body:
The Windows registry contains paths telling Windows where your special folders
(Documents, Desktop, Pictures) live. After migration, these need to be updated
to point at the new location so that all applications find your files.

Skipping this means:
- File Explorer will still show the OLD location as Documents, Desktop etc.
- Applications like Office, browser downloads will save to the OLD location
- Your migration will be functionally incomplete

Only skip if you are managing the registry update separately with another tool.
skip_registry_update.risk: HIGH if skipped — apps will not find your files in the new location.
skip_registry_update.example: You are using a third-party tool to update the registry. Choose Y.
skip_registry_update.recommended: N (do not skip) — always update the registry

create_symlink.title: Create Symlink at Source
create_symlink.body:
A symbolic link (symlink) is a special folder that acts as a redirect.
If created at the old source location, any app that still tries to use
the old path will be transparently redirected to the new location.

This is a compatibility aid for older software that ignores the registry
and uses hardcoded paths like C:\Users\John\Documents.
create_symlink.risk: LOW — symlinks are transparent to applications.
create_symlink.example: Old software always saves to C:\Users\John\Documents. Symlink redirects it to D:\.
create_symlink.recommended: N for most users. Y if you have old software with hardcoded paths.

enable_checkpoint.title: Checkpoint / Resume
enable_checkpoint.body:
If the migration is interrupted (power cut, laptop lid closed, network drop)
checkpointing records which files were already copied.

When you re-run the script, it picks up from where it left off instead
of starting over from the beginning. Essential for large migrations over
network shares or slow connections.
enable_checkpoint.risk: ZERO — checkpointing only adds a small log file.
enable_checkpoint.example: You are migrating 500GB over Wi-Fi overnight. Enable checkpoint in case it drops.
enable_checkpoint.recommended: Y for large migrations (>50GB) or network destinations

schedule_task.title: Scheduled Task
schedule_task.body:
Creates a Windows Scheduled Task so the migration runs automatically
at a set time without you needing to open the script manually.

Useful for:
- Recurring backups (FullProfileBackup mode)
- Running during off-hours when the PC is idle

NOTE: Tasks run as SYSTEM by default. SYSTEM cannot access OneDrive,
email credentials, or your personal registry hive (HKCU).
For email notifications or OneDrive interaction, choose 'Current user' as RunAs.
schedule_task.risk: LOW — task can be deleted anytime from Task Scheduler.
schedule_task.example: You want a weekly backup every Sunday at 10 PM. Enable task, set Weekly, 22:00.
schedule_task.recommended: Y for recurring FullProfileBackup. N for one-time migrations.

secure_wipe.title: Secure Wipe Source
secure_wipe.body:
After copying files to the destination, this option overwrites the
original files at the source with random data before deleting them.

This makes recovery with forensic tools impossible.

WARNING — THIS IS IRREVERSIBLE:
- Files cannot be recovered after secure wipe
- Even professional data recovery tools cannot retrieve wiped files
- Only use this if you are intentionally decommissioning the source drive

Requires Microsoft SDelete tool (auto-downloaded if missing).
secure_wipe.risk: CRITICAL — permanent data destruction. Cannot be undone.
secure_wipe.example: Decommissioning an old laptop being sold. Wipe source after migrating.
secure_wipe.recommended: N for almost all users. Y only when decommissioning hardware.

validate_only.title: Validate-Only Mode
validate_only.body:
Runs all pre-flight checks (disk space, permissions, KFM status, VSS,
folder accessibility) without copying a single file.

Difference from Dry Run:
- Dry Run simulates the full copy and produces a report
- Validate Only just checks prerequisites — much faster

Use Validate Only to quickly confirm the script CAN run before you
commit to a long migration.
validate_only.example: Quick check before a 2AM scheduled migration to make sure nothing is blocked.
validate_only.recommended: N during normal use. Y for pre-flight checks before long runs.

pilot_user.title: Pilot User
pilot_user.body:
When ALL users mode is selected, Pilot User processes only ONE named user
first as a test before proceeding with the rest.

Useful for IT administrators doing a staged rollout:
1. Run with pilot user to verify everything works
2. Review the report
3. Re-run without pilot user to process everyone

Leave blank to process all selected users without a pilot run.
pilot_user.risk: LOW — only limits scope, does not change what happens.
pilot_user.example: You are migrating 50 PCs. Pilot on one user first to verify your config.
pilot_user.recommended: Blank for personal PCs. Use for enterprise rollouts.

power_user_exclusions.title: Folder / Pattern Exclusions
power_user_exclusions.body:
Exclude specific folders or file patterns from being migrated.
Comma-separated. Supports wildcards.

Examples:
  node_modules, .git, *.tmp, Temp

Auto-exclusions (enabled by default) already exclude:
  AppData\Local\Temp, $Recycle.Bin, thumbs.db, desktop.ini

Disabling auto-exclusions is not recommended — it causes the script
to try copying system-locked and irrelevant junk files.
power_user_exclusions.risk: LOW — excluded items are simply skipped.
power_user_exclusions.example: Your Documents has a huge node_modules folder you do not want to migrate.
power_user_exclusions.recommended: Leave blank unless you have specific large folders to exclude.

bitlocker_required.title: Require BitLocker
bitlocker_required.body:
BitLocker is Windows disk encryption. If this option is enabled,
the script will CHECK that the destination drive is BitLocker-encrypted
before starting. If not encrypted, the script aborts.

Use this in environments where data security policy requires that
backup destinations must always be encrypted at rest.

Checking if BitLocker is on: open File Explorer, right-click the drive.
If you see 'Turn on BitLocker' it is OFF. If you see 'Manage BitLocker' it is ON.
bitlocker_required.risk: LOW — only blocks the run if the destination is unencrypted.
bitlocker_required.example: Your company policy says all backup drives must be encrypted.
bitlocker_required.recommended: N for home users. Y for regulated environments.

wsl_install_root.title: WSL Install Root
wsl_install_root.body:
WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) lets you run Linux on Windows.
If you have WSL distros (Ubuntu, Debian, etc.) installed, FullProfileBackup
backs them up and RestoreProfile can re-install them.

This setting controls WHERE WSL distros are restored to on the target machine.
Default C:\WSL works for most setups.

If your WSL distros were on a different drive (e.g. D:\WSL), enter that path.
wsl_install_root.risk: LOW — only affects WSL restore location.
wsl_install_root.example: Your WSL was on D:\WSL to save C: space. Enter: D:\WSL
wsl_install_root.recommended: Leave as C:\WSL unless you know your WSL was installed elsewhere.

network_timeout.title: Network Timeout
network_timeout.body:
When migrating to a network share (UNC path like \\server\share),
this controls how long the script waits for a response before giving up.

Default 30 seconds works for most local networks.
Increase for slow WAN links, VPN connections, or unreliable networks.
Decrease for fast local networks where 30s would be an unnecessary wait.
network_timeout.risk: LOW — only affects how quickly failures are detected.
network_timeout.example: Migrating over a slow VPN to a remote file server. Increase to 120.
network_timeout.recommended: 30 for local network. 60-120 for VPN or slow links.

glossary.title: Glossary of Terms
glossary.body:
VSS       Volume Shadow Copy Service — reads locked/open files
KFM       Known Folder Move — OneDrive feature that redirects Desktop/Docs/Pics to cloud
Robocopy  Windows built-in file copy tool with retry and verification
Checksum  A fingerprint of a file used to verify it copied correctly (SHA256/SHA1/MD5)
Shell folders  Special Windows folders: Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Music, Pictures, Videos
SID       Security Identifier — unique ID for a Windows user account
Hive      A section of the Windows registry (HKCU = current user, HKLM = machine)
ACL       Access Control List — file/folder permissions
Symlink   Symbolic link — a folder that transparently redirects to another location
BitLocker Windows disk encryption built into Pro/Enterprise editions
WSL       Windows Subsystem for Linux — run Linux apps on Windows
UNC path  Network path in format \\server\share\folder
DPAPI     Windows credential encryption tied to your user account
MFA/2FA   Multi-Factor Authentication — requires app password for SMTP access
App Password  A secondary password generated by your email provider for script access

confirm_execute.title: Confirm and Execute
confirm_execute.body:
You are about to start the actual operation.

Before proceeding, check:
- Destination path is correct and has enough free space
- You have reviewed what mode was selected and understand what it does
- If this is a first run, consider using Dry Run mode first

Once you press Y and Enter, the script will begin immediately.
You can press Ctrl+C at any time to abort — already-copied files
will remain at the destination but the operation will be incomplete.
confirm_execute.risk: Depends on your chosen mode — see mode description above.
confirm_execute.example: Everything looks good. Press Y to begin.
confirm_execute.recommended: Review the summary above before confirming.

run_window.title: How to Run the Main Script
run_window.body:
Option 1 — Current window: output appears here. Closing this window stops the script.
Option 2 — New window: a new PowerShell window opens. This window stays open.
Option 3 — New window + wait: a new window opens and this window waits for it to finish.

For large migrations (hours), use option 2 or 3 so you can monitor progress.
For scheduled tasks or quick runs, option 1 is simplest.
run_window.risk: LOW — this only affects how the window is managed.
run_window.example: Large overnight migration. Use option 2 so you can close this wizard window.
run_window.recommended: 1 for quick runs. 2 or 3 for long migrations.
